Houthis claim attack on Saudi oil refinery, blasts shake Riyadh
item.description:
Yemen’s Houthis said they targeted Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil refinery with a ballistic missile on Tuesday, as blasts shook the capital of the world’s top crude exporter.
Saudi Arabia, the Middle East’s largest economy, has suffered weeks of strikes from the Iran-backed Houthis against oil and civilian sites including Riyadh’s international airport.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces were able to target the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, saying the strike caused “massive fires.”
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis earlier said it had shot down three missiles fired by the group towards the Eastern Province.
A resident in the city of Al Khobar, south of the Ras Tanura complex, told AFP he heard explosions around dawn and received a text message alert.
“We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang,” the resident said.
Maritime security agency Vanguard said a fire was reported in the Ras Tanura area in the early hours of Tuesday after an attack.
“The fire has reportedly been contained, while the extent of damage and any impact on oil-loading operations remain unclear at current,” Vanguard said.
The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia’s Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and a cornerstone of the kingdom’s energy sector.
The complex has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by strikes blamed on Iran, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.
Meanwhile a series of explosions echoed across the capital, Riyadh, shaking office windows in the city center. A text message alert warned residents to seek shelter.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted two ballistic missiles that were fired at Riyadh.
Earlier, a Houthi official said the Egyptian parliament’s decision to authorize defensive military support for Saudi Arabia amounted to a declaration of war.
Egypt’s parliament authorized the measure on Monday, following a request from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
“It is truly remarkable that while these people go to discuss what they call ‘peace in the region,’ Egypt and its parliament declare support for the so-called defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, declare war against the Republic of Yemen,” said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, in a Telegram post.
It was not clear exactly what support was on offer from Egypt, which has the Arab world’s largest military.
Al-Houthi’s statement also pointed to Monday’s visit to Tehran by the Saudi defense minister, Pakistan’s army chief and Turkiye’s intelligence chief, in a bid to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East war.
Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad recently signed a Nato-style defense pact in Mecca, pledging to consider an attack on one country as an attack on all three.
Turkiye and Pakistan have not announced any strikes on the Houthis during the group’s weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Al-Houthi said the group was “not afraid of any alliance that may be formed.”
Yemen’s largely dormant conflict reignited in July, further destabilizing the region months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.
The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing swathes of Red Sea coastline in a major offensive in September.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.
This month the Houthis ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, forcing the cancellation of flagship events and shutting down Riyadh’s airport for two weeks.
The Houthis’ war with the Saudi-led coalition began in 2015, months after they ousted the internationally recognized government from the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

item.title: India media groups challenge new data privacy rules in top court
item.description:
India’s Supreme Court on Tuesday sought the government’s response to a challenge by news publishers who say changes to data privacy rules threaten press freedom.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government introduced the rules last year to guide the law to strengthen personal data protection, but critics say their sweeping scope risks undermining public interest reporting.
The new rules “fail to provide any exemption in favor of journalistic activity” and “threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity,” according to the petition by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents some of India’s biggest news organizations.
They include Network18, part of the Reliance conglomerate led by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, and NDTV, owned by the Adani Group, founded by Gautam Adani -- two tycoons who are both close to Modi.
“We think it could have an impact on investigative journalism and compromise sources,” Sujata Gupta of the DNPA told AFP.
Data privacy laws in several parts of the world, including the European Union, provide specific exemptions for journalism.
The law’s requirement to disclose all personal data processed, without a public interest exemption, would “seriously hinder investigative reporting and could discourage whistleblowers from coming forward,” international media watchdog Reporters Without Borders said in a statement.
Independent activists and smaller news organizations have also challenged provisions removing exemptions for personal information sought under India’s Right To Information (RTI) transparency law.
“The removal of the public interest override... of the RTI Act now allows information offices of the government to withhold information that is deemed ‘personal’ even if it has significant connection to a public activity or public interest,” argues a legal challenge filed by investigative news website, The Reporters’ Collective.
Critics have long accused Modi’s Hindu nationalist government of undermining press freedom, a charge it denies. The court will next hear the matter on November 17.

item.title: Norway, Finland leaders hold ‘frank and substantive’ talk with Putin
item.description:
Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister held a “frank and substantive” discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday about efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Nordic leaders said.
“The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The statement noted that the call had been “held in consultation with Ukraine” and followed a meeting in Oslo on October 20 between Store, Stubb and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as US envoy Steve Witkoff.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the meeting remotely.
After the Oslo talks, Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg to meet Putin.
Stubb and Store initiated Tuesday’s call to discuss “efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe,” their statement said.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation,” Store said.
Stubb described the discussion between the three as “frank and substantive.”
Shortly after the announcement of the call, Kyiv said Zelensky had spoken to the Nordic leaders about the conversation with Putin.
Stubb confirmed the talks with Zelensky in a social media post and commented: “Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace.”
The leaders stressed that they were representing their own countries and had not spoken on behalf of Europe, but Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen bemoaned that they had gone “solo.”
“I’m very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn’t been coordinated with any of the rest of us,” she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders, including Store and Stubb, in Finland.
“I honestly don’t know what those two countries think they can achieve with this,” she said.
Relations between Ukraine and the United States have become strained again after Trump this month suddenly announced a deal with Russia for diesel, as part of his efforts to lower oil prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Ukraine reacted with dismay after Trump also waived sanctions against Russia and appeared to again pivot to Putin.
The Oslo meeting followed furious diplomatic efforts in Washington, Kyiv and Western capitals to calm the situation.
Norway and Finland, both Nato members, share borders with Russia and the statement emphasised that the countries are “firm supporters of Ukraine.”

item.title: UN: Greenhouse gas levels hit new record highs in 2025
item.description:
Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to new record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries to come, the United Nations said Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the UN’s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO’s 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, running from November 9 to 20.
“Another year, another new record,” said WMO deputy secretary-general Ko Barrett.
“Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.
“The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries.”
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them respectively to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66 percent of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the “recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino,” the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
“However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning.”
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.
“We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024,” Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16 percent of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.
The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems towards decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
Primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution, SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades.
Why H2 levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

item.title: Rizvi: IGP’s crossfire remarks have put govt in an awkward position
item.description:
BNP acting secretary general Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Tuesday said the Inspector General of Police’s (IGP) remarks about reinstating crossfire have caused unease within the government.
“We feel deeply saddened that the head of the police force, who is part of the government, would talk about crossfire. If it was a slip of the tongue, that would be a different matter. But such remarks put the government in an awkward position,” he said.
Rizvi made the remarks while inaugurating a free medical camp in front of the BNP’s central office at Naya Paltan, Dhaka, marking the 48th founding anniversary of Jatiotabadi Jubo Dal.
Rizvi said there are adequate laws to combat terrorism and crime, and law enforcement agencies are responsible for enforcing those.
He said the country endured 17 years of what he described as inhumane misrule involving crossfire killings, enforced disappearances, secret killings and bloodshed.
After years of struggle against such practices, the country experienced the July uprising and August 5, followed by the BNP coming to power through a free and fair electoral process, he said.
Rizvi said people across the country expect a humane Bangladesh under Tarique Rahman’s leadership, adding that such remarks from the head of a law enforcement agency are deeply concerning.
Rizvi said Tarique Rahman’s commitment to building a humane Bangladesh was reflected in initiatives such as the Family Card and Farmers’ Card, and canal excavation programs.
He said these initiatives are aimed at making Bangladesh a more liveable country, describing this as a central part of Tarique Rahman’s vision and development plan.
Referring to concerns about rising juvenile delinquency and crime in several areas of Dhaka, he said he believes the police force has many honest and capable officers who can effectively tackle crime if allowed to work.
“If the law is properly enforced without any influence, crime can be eliminated from society,” he said.
Rizvi said extrajudicial methods could never be an effective way to control crime, whether through enforced disappearances or crossfire killings.
Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md Ali Hossain Fakir on Monday said police might resort to crossfire if the government allows it and it becomes necessary to maintain law and order and curb crimes.

Here is how you can save your electricity bill
item.description:
A refrigerator accounts for a large share of household electricity use, mainly because it runs 24 hours a day. Even minor mistakes in how it is used can noticeably inflate the monthly bill. According to experts, using the appliance properly can cut power consumption significantly.
Many people assume that only old refrigerators guzzle electricity. In reality, a few common mistakes can lead to wasted power in both new and old models. Regular maintenance and mindful use, those concerned say, are the most effective ways to save energy.
Experts stress that a refrigerator’s efficiency depends not only on the quality of the machine but also on the habits of the user. Following a few simple rules can lower your electricity bill and extend the life of the appliance.
Organize the interior When items are easy to find, the door does not have to stay open for long, so less cold air escapes.
Don’t keep the fridge completely empty A fridge with a moderate amount of food holds its temperature better than an entirely empty one.
Defrost regularly If your fridge does not have no-frost technology, excess ice can build up in the freezer and increase power consumption. The ice should be cleared at regular intervals.
Keep the vents clear Blocking the vents with food prevents cold air from circulating evenly, putting extra strain on the cooling system.
Keep the door shut during power cuts During load-shedding or an outage, keeping the door closed helps the fridge stay cold for much longer.
Allow air to circulate around the fridge Placing the fridge flush against a wall or furniture makes it harder for heat to escape, which can increase electricity use.
Choose the right size Using a refrigerator far larger than your family needs can result in unnecessary power consumption.
Experts say saving electricity requires mindful use of all household appliances, not just the fridge. But because a refrigerator never switches off, even small adjustments can add up to substantial savings in the long run.
They also suggest that if a refrigerator is very old or breaks down frequently, it may be worth considering a modern, energy-efficient model. With proper use and regular maintenance, households can lower their monthly bills while keeping their fridge in good working condition for years.

item.title: Do these five things every morning, and your memory may thank you at 80
item.description:
Mornings are rarely calm. Work deadlines, school runs, family duties and a dozen small chores leave little room for a quiet routine of one’s own.
Yet a 2025 survey by Nespresso and Project Healthy Minds found that nearly 90% of people believe the early moments of the day directly affect their mood and mental wellbeing for the rest of it.
Medical experts say the first few hours do more than lift the mood. They may also be key to protecting long-term brain health and keeping memory and thinking sharp into old age.
During sleep, the brain carries out a kind of overnight cleaning operation. Dr Eva L Feldman, a neurologist at the University of Michigan, explains that brain cells clear out waste while we sleep.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, this cleaning network is known as the glymphatic system, which uses fluid to flush harmful waste out of brain cells. The result is that the brain is at its freshest and sharpest soon after waking.
Dr Majid Fotuhi, a neuroscientist at the Brain Institute, says the first hour after waking sets the tone for the whole day. To keep the brain active and healthy over the long term, he recommends building five simple habits into the morning.
Taking on stress straight after waking is bad for the brain, says Dr Fotuhi. Prolonged stress releases the hormone cortisol, and high levels of it can damage cells in the hippocampus, the brain’s main center for learning and memory. Staying calm and optimistic in the morning therefore matters.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) suggests several ways to ease morning stress:
Rather than jumping up the moment the alarm rings, experts advise lying quietly for a few minutes and asking yourself a question.
Dr Fotuhi suggests: “How can I make today enjoyable?”
This is also a good moment to think about how to fit the five pillars of brain health into your day: exercise, a balanced diet, adequate sleep, stress management and intellectual stimulation. Doing so makes it easier to organize the day and keeps your mood buoyant.
Mental exercise early in the day stimulates the brain’s nerve cells, according to Dr Feldman. Reading, journaling, or solving puzzles such as sudoku and crosswords can sharpen the mind from the start of the day.
Dr Fotuhi also recommends writing down three intentions in a notebook each morning:
Morning exercise helps boost the performance of nerve cells, says Dr Feldman. Walking, running, cycling, swimming or yoga all improve blood flow to the brain. Exercise done in a group, through team sports or social activity, can also help preserve brain age.
A 2024 study published in the journal GeroScience found that 12 weeks of strength or resistance training produced structural changes in the hippocampus. These changes enhance neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to learn new things.
A breakfast rich in protein and fibre, with tea or coffee, is an excellent way to begin the day. Foods that are part of the mind diet in particular are well documented as helping to slow brain decline.
Adding leafy greens, nuts, olive oil, berries, chicken and fish to your morning meal supplies the brain with nutrients and helps preserve memory.
Dr Feldman stresses that it is never too late to start looking after the brain. Damage from smoking, drinking, or an irregular lifestyle becomes hard to reverse once symptoms appear.
The brain’s greatest strength, he notes, is neuroplasticity, meaning it can be rewired and strengthened at any age. These five small morning habits, practiced daily, could determine how sharp your memory and intellect remain in the years ahead.

item.title: Dr Yunus, other Asian humanitarians globally rank as ‘21st Century Merit Icons’
item.description:
Bangladesh's Nobel laureate and former chief adviser to the interim government Dr Muhammad Yunus has been indexed in a group of Asian notables recognized by the Britain-based merit-indexing body Impact Hallmarks (IH) as the 'Century Merit Icons'.
IH has named 38 individuals the 'The Merit Sovereigns of 21st Century', scored against a 1,000-point framework designed to reward documented achievement over public visibility.
Around eleven Asian icons appear in the top three of eight of the ten thematic categories, and fifteen more feature in the wider recognition tiers.
Nepal's Pushpa Basnet, China's Chen Si and Japan's Yukio Shige jointly secure 3rd place in 'Humanitarianism and Social Justice', while from Pakistan, late Bilquis Edhi tops the Legacy Memorial category and Arch-polymath Prof Aurangzeb Hafi secures a shared first place in 'Scientific Endeavours' category.
Unveiled in the Quarticentennial Merited Impacts Gazette (2000–2025), the list is billed as the first merit-based retrospective of the century's first quarter.
From an initial pool of 1.9 million notables across 195 countries, 150 independent assessors shortlisted 187 individuals using the Merited Impact Value (MIV) framework.
It weighs documentary evidence, systemic transformation and public resonance across four dimensions: Humanitarian Impact Merit (HIM), Scientific Impact Merit (SIM), Resilience Impact Merit (RIM) and Cumulative Impact Merit (CIM).
A global online poll served as a public validation layer.
Described by IH as the 'Arch-Polymath of 21st Century', Prof Aurangzeb Hafi is recognized in three categories.
In 'Scientific Endeavours', he shares first place with physicist Dr Fritjof Capra (US) on 950+ points.
He was cited for integrating the scientific pentarchy, identifying the alarming mega-toxification of underground water reserves caused by prevailing sewage-drainage practices in underdeveloped countries, for developing the 'Deca-Archic Phygital Literacy Model' and discovering the phenomenon of Magneto-Hydro-Tropism (MHT).
In Multiple Iconicities he is placed at second with 957 points for being a cross-disciplinary 'Arch-researcher', who integrates research across 93 epistemic subject-fields, behind James Harrison (Australia—965) and ahead of Nathan Myhrvold (US—945).
In Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons he placed third with 910 points, behind King Charles III (930) and physicist John Preskill (US—925).
Bilquis Edhi (Pakistan—965) leads the posthumous Legacy Memorial category for her Jhoola project, which provided shelter and medical care to abandoned infants.
Peter Higgs (UK—950) and Kofi Annan (Ghana—930) complete the top three. In Humanitarianism and Social Justice, three Asians share third place on 930+ points.
Yukio Shige (Japan), known as the 'Chotto Matte' ('wait a moment' man), leads volunteers credited with saving more than 750 people from suicide at the Tōjinbō cliffs.
Chen Si (China) also prevented hundreds of suicides. Pushpa Basnet (Nepal) founded organizations rescuing children who would otherwise grow up in prison with incarcerated parents.
In Scientific Endeavours, Fields Medalist Shing-Tung Yau (China) and H.E. Dr Mohamed Al-Kuwaiti (UAE) share second place on 920+ with Noam Chomsky and Dana Bolles (both US).
Cosmologist Prof. Chandra Wickramasinghe (Sri Lanka) is third on 910. Ghanim Al-Muftah (Qatar—939) places second in Luminary and Differently-Able Icons, behind Nick Vujicic (Australia/US—940).
Siti Atikoh Supriyanti (Indonesia—907), recognized for community-centred public health advocacy, features in Dignified Asceticism.
Bana Al-Abed (Syria—905), whose social media dispatches from besieged Aleppo drew international attention, is third among Young Trailblazing Icons.
The overall topper of the Gazette is Stephen Soldz (US—967), who leads Humanitarianism and Social Justice for documenting psychological coercion tactics used against war prisoners.
He was the first ethicist to make academic condemnation of employing the sacred religious texts as an instrument of torture.
Francesca Albanese (Italy) and Graça Machel (Mozambique) share second on 940+ points.
Albanese, United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, is recognized for her 2024 report "Anatomy of Genocide" and for facing sanctions over her work, while Machel is recognized for providing baselines for the UN's revolutionary research work on the effects of war on children.
Pope Francis (Vatican City—940) leads Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity, followed by Capra (935) and Greta Thunberg (Sweden-933).
Greta Thunberg is recognized for the arc running from her solitary school strike movement to leading the high-risk flotilla missions carrying aid toward Gaza including the Freedom Flotilla in June 2025 and the 44-nation Global Sumud Flotilla in September 2025, the interception of which led to 450 activists being detained, and sparked protests across three continents.
Tarja Halonen (Finland—920), Machel and Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand) lead Dignified Asceticism.
Usain Bolt (Jamaica—905), LeBron James (US—903) and Cristiano Ronaldo (Portugal—902) top Athletics and Physical Excellence.
Orion Jean (US—935) and Greta Thunberg (920) head the Young Trailblazing Icons.
Pakistan's Dr Amjad Saqib, Sri Lanka's Jehan Perera, India's Arunima Sinha and the two young Pakistani siblings Fiddhah Hafiah and Ghulam Bishar Hafi are jointly heralded as the 'Five-pointed Asian Star'.
The results form part of the 'Sovereign Sesquicentennial Confluence of Intellect & Impact' (2026).
Full results would be archived in the Quarticentennial Merited Impacts Gazette, alongside the Quarticentennial Roll of Honour (HI©) to be published in due course.

item.description:
“Why does so little of Bangladesh’s contemporary art history survive anywhere except someone’s old Facebook album?” was one of the questions Sarridon Collective explored in their exhibition ‘triggered after s*x’, held at Daagi Art Garage from August 1–8,2026.
Months after it closed, those questions and the discussions around them still ruminate in my head.
The show looked not so much at tragedy as at the moments that come after, what Marx, extending Hegel, calls the tragedy that comes the second time as farce. The revolutionary moment dissolves, short-lived, and disillusionment follows right on the dopamine hit.
A bitter reminder to prepare for what’s to come.
Instead of relief there is greater tension; before we can process one tragedy, we are met with events of multiplied severity.
There is little possibility for a ‘post’-traumatic experience, because stress persists.
Looking at the hyperactive happenings of this ongoing melodrama, at tragedies dimmed by newer technologies of infrastructure and media, at our isolated strategies to mute our own weeping, feels, in retrospect, humorous.
Photo: Courtesy
I’d call this humor defiance or resistance, if those terms had not been used elsewhere to build the very thing the humor in this exhibit responds to.
In the post-politically correct era, where we have internalized the language of possible accusations and deniability, the jester’s joke stands elsewhere entirely.
It does not accuse or defend; it simply passes, reveals its truth, and acknowledges unspoken truths ostracised by, and outside of, old and emerging narratives.
It does not live in opposition, so it never loses its footing.
The exhibit, featuring artists Imran Firdaus, Shikdar Shaikat, Fahad Hossain Kazmee and Nafees Sabur, looks at national trauma through this joke, well aware of its own tendencies to self-censor and repress.
The trauma is now transnationalized. Shaikat’s illustrations reiterate the language of oppression through ridicule, lifting the veil on the close-knit habitus between neoliberalism and MAGA.
Kazmee’s paintings allude to the materiality of trauma through a missile piercing the vertebrae.
Sabur’s prose compositions on the mundane life of tragedy testify to structural violence in a subjectivity that changes its register as the political absurdities play out.
Firdaus’s video essay plays 13 film openings from 1972, in the newly formed nation, against the audio of the ongoing state radio, which somehow syncs on its own, offering the viewer a way to trace a pattern of origin and look at the self within.
The censored sex in the title, achieved through the asterisk, pulls the word out of the regular, otherwise mundane at best and medical at worst, and foreshadows the censorships the show wishes to talk about.
I visited twice and still couldn’t explore every artwork, , each visit a round trip of more than 30 km.
Between industrial buildings and tanneries in Hazaribag, a few minutes from the Buriganga, the show was inaugurated with a Constitution cake on an August afternoon, close to two years since the “mass uprising”.
What appealed to me immediately and lingered longest were Firdaus’s text cards, a cross between a guerrilla exhibition and a homage to love letters, written from the precipice of coming to terms with the precipice itself.
They are scattered on the floor like the ‘abashik hotel’ brothel adverts found on city footpaths and footbridges. The cards announce and confess poignant truths.
Their acceptance of our shared predicament echoes as the late-late-stage capitalist successor of chopping wood and carrying water; it is either the result of enlightenment or the path to it.
One card, in an omniscient voice, says “You are in tension because you lose attention”, which may suggest that tension comes from the body’s restlessness and inability to focus, in an economy where attention is currency, or it may point to an existential crisis of being unseen, the anxiety of evanescence.
“Ami tomar phone er bhetor ekbar ghure ashte chai” (I want to explore inside your phone once) replaces “mon” (the simple Bengali word for the unified spirit of the heart and mind, unconcerned with Cartesian dualism) with “phone” in a popular 2009 Bangla pop song.
Appropriately revised for a rapidly transforming era, where we still yearn for love (and suspect infidelity) even beneath a global technofascist, transhumanist project.
This doesn’t make the device an alternative to the heart.
It shows they are synonymous, and how we weave technologies into the emotional and the unconscious, producing newer forms of subjectivity.
It is not a mere moralistic critique of ‘consumption’, much as David Graeber rejects the reductive assumption that people are passive victims of products.
Firdaus’s wordplay is not a literal replacement of the real with the internet-mediated mechanical; it shows how technological artefacts hold the most human and visceral things: desire, insecurity, restlessness, longing. It also reminds me of his one-line poem, “Attyar shathe jantrik shomporko” (mechanical relationship with the soul), or, bent slightly, “jontrer shathe attik shomporko” (a soul relationship with the machine).
You find humor again in Shaikat’s digital collage “Porimoni Suffering From Severe Fever”, framed next to Firdaus’s vintage cinema clips.
The series tells of a plague that has captured the metropolis, in partly absurdist and partly Kafkaesque satire. Porimoni’s fever is treated like a state of emergency; chairs and table fans are “living”, going through the predicaments of the masses, grappling with depression and culture wars.
Some of the text will be familiar to the chronically online.
Photo: Courtesy
It is taken from real Facebook posts and comments, which stand alone as commentary on social realities, no longer bound to their creators.
One text, “the woman’s work is to stay at home and raise children”, appears with the wrong Bengali consonants, exactly as the original commenter posted it, which undeniably adds humor.
It reflects a tragic reality, but plays more as farce.
What catches the audience’s attention most is Shaikat’s book installation at the centre, laid on a table, wrapped in styrofoam and plastic like packaged meat, with photographs of raw beef and chicken on the cover.
This hyperreality brings unease, reminding us that nondegradable plastic almost immortalizes this period of our lives, full of inconvenient conveniences.
Who could have guessed the Kali Yuga would be so characterized by simulacra?
On the next wall, Kazmee paints the state of the corporeal in the Kali Yuga, the remains of ethnonationalist violence.
‘Anatomy of Hunger’ shows nameless skeletons, missiles, rubble and blood, and the multispecies scrambling in the ruins.
The fish, the bird, the crocodile have evolved into their deformation.
The monster in one painting has a nationalist icon for an eye. Kazmee’s thesis is quite straightforward. His hungry, consuming subject is far removed from those in the other artworks.
As Graeber reminds us, to consume means to use up, to “eat up, devour, waste, destroy, or spend”; and in Hegel’s view, we differ from other animals in desiring from lack.
The paradox in the master/slave dialectic relates to what Kazmee presents in his paintings of obliteration: what it means to really consume.
I had initially overlooked the series by the entrance, overwhelmed by the Bangla text that filled most of each composition, but revisiting it struck me.
Sabur’s series is, for lack of a better word, relatable to the citizens of this young and restless state.
His line on post-July iconoclasm and replacing the ‘fascist icon’ with new sculptures memorializing the movement related closely to my own work, which was fun to see; the fun is furthered by the text above a pixelated apple, “I enjoy being bitten but not all the time”.
Sabur’s prose plucks from the new political project, a gruesome news story that citizens have grown accustomed to and numb to.
Sabur’s series faces Shaikat’s on parallel walls.
They mirror each other, both satirizing the imperialist project, neoliberal ‘norms’ in bed with looming fundamentalism, and internet-induced culture wars, from a male subjectivity that suits the digital medium.
Mediums are tacit; they communicate before we can identify them.
Their work also shares a sense of the struggle and confusion that constructs and challenges masculinity. Shaikat’s choice to centre Porimoni, a widely ‘trolled’ yet desired public figure, connotes that impulse.
Perhaps it is most directly addressed by Sabur, in “us male tortoises”.
The male subjectivity is important, since it acts as the medium for the political theatre of the nation-state and urban life, which photographer Rahul Talukdar might call “Dhaka Opera”.
Men’s trauma, economic and sexual, goes unacknowledged, lacking language in legal and media discourse that refuses to even name it.
And since representation takes precedence in the drive for development and progress, perhaps what we need is a revised representation of men, and a revised understanding of themselves to themselves.
In “The Past That Never Told Me Its Name”, Firdaus’s five-minute stitch of the opening one to two minutes of 13 found films, out of the 29 released in newly independent Bangladesh in 1972, offers a space for introspection.
We see national trauma expressed through the local practice of melodrama, and the unavailability of the other 16 films raises the question of what survives and what was worth keeping as archive.
The audio comes from a radio set playing the state broadcast.
On the table beside the screen are copies of two legal documents: “The Censorship of Flims act,1963” and “The Cinematograph Act, 1918”. The clips are left as they are, “with no narrator telling you what to think”, as are the documents, but it still evokes a small grin.
“Political memory in Bangladesh does not only wound,” Firdaus writes in the concept note Satire and the Return of the Repressed , “it also produces absurdity, running jokes, the humour of a population that has learned to read between the lines of official language”.
The joke can only claim to be a joke, nothing more, and simultaneously a “confession dressed as comedy”.
I also think about the afterlife of the joke. But if archiving is what we do (or in some cases don’t do) with art, what about the joke?
When tools of resistance like art are co-opted, I think the same done to jokes fails far more miserably.
Appropriated humor becomes a sort of kitsch that does not quite trigger sincere, involuntary laughter and, at best, produces a simulation of it, a desire to be a part of it.
We see this in political cartoons, where genuine humor hardly gels with hypocrisy.
By the time such a cartoon is exploited as a centrepiece of a new narrative, the artist has already moved on to ridicule it, as the work of cartoonist Mehedi Haque may show.
Jokes reveal tacit truths, and their inherent refusal or inability to conform lets even the most self-censored subjects embody resistance beyond ideology.
“The exhibition,” Firdaus writes, “stands as the obscene, unserious cousin of testimony: no less political for being funny, no less true for arriving after the fact”.
Whether Sarridon Collective intended the show as a vehicle for somatic relief, satire, or both, its ability to sit with our own suffering and precarity is freeing.
This acceptance points towards the possibility of a spiritual life, giving a visual language to the complex, confusing predicaments we are still enduring.
The audience is allowed to touch the art, and its tactility, like the laughter the jokes may trigger, attempts to remind us of something about being human.
Maybe it is through suffering the profane that we can access the profound, not in spite of it. The show does not promise catharsis, but it can provoke a chuckle or laughter.
And that singular trigger might just be enough.
Ohama Raaz is a visual artist.

item.title: Desert flower
item.description:
O David, stop measuring the desert flowers
How long will the marigolds be measured by your fine veins?
The storm is whimpering for you, and a little rain
On a barren land yearning for you to return,
How long will the lilies be measured by your fine veins?
The Orange Globemallows are not burning in the sun, but in your fire.
Listen to the estranged Cactuses, David.
They carved your fine veins with warmth, water, and red.
Hardy, woody, and lovely they are!
How long will you protect them from your fine veins, David?
Suraya Akter prefers short poems; everything she writes is a draft except her poetry.

item.title: Faith has teeth
item.description:
I dyed my hair black last night.
This morning the sun came in like an accusation.
Yesterday I was blue and green,
all bruise and algae,
looking older than I am,
wiser than I wanted to be,
lost in the particular way
only the nearly-grown can be.
But this morning
I looked in the mirror
and she was gone.
Three months of blue,
three months of green,
three months of becoming someone
I could not recognise
were washed out by black.
My face looked younger.
Not beautiful.
Not happier.
Just younger.
Four years younger, almost.
I have not been fourteen in five years,
but there she was,
wearing my face again,
with the same foolish eyes,
the same mouth that had not yet learned
how often a promise can rot.
How strange
to look less lost
and feel more lost for it.
Yesterday I looked like someone
who had survived something.
Today I look like someone
who still believes she won't.
And isn't that the cruelest part?
At fourteen,
I had already decided my destiny.
I had named the roads,
picked the doors,
counted the years ahead of me
as though the future were a house
I could simply walk into.
I thought faith
was another word for knowing.
I did not know
faith could betray you.
I did not know
the girl who planned her life at fourteen
would grow up only to watch it
quietly become someone else's.
So here I am,
black-haired again,
four years older
and somehow four years younger,
standing in the morning light
looking like the girl I was
before the world taught me
that destiny is a liar
with a beautiful voice.
And God,
how young she looks.
How terrible
that she still looks like me.
Nubisha Rabya Topote, an XI-grade student at Holy Cross College, is a poet and writer

item.title: Fire erupts from ground in Cox’s Bazar, three units deployed
item.description:
A fire broke out from the ground in Inani, a tourist area in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar, while workers were excavating the site to install a tube well on Tuesday. Smoke and a gas-like smell were also reported, raising suspicions that underground gas may have fuelled the blaze.
Three fire service units were deployed to the site and were working to bring the fire under control.
The fire erupted around 8:30am near a small bridge in Inani.
Saidul Islam, station officer at Ukhiya Fire Service, confirmed the incident, saying firefighters reached the scene after receiving the report. He said the cause of the fire was still being investigated, although the preliminary suspicion was that gas beneath the surface might be responsible.
Meanwhile, electricity supply along a 15km stretch of the 33kV power line, from Monkhali to Patuartek, was temporarily suspended over concerns that the fire could spread to electrical infrastructure, according to Ukhiya Palli Bidyut Samity.
The incident triggered panic among local residents.
Al-Amin, an employee of a five-star hotel near the site, said several hotel staff members lived in a room beside the area where the fire broke out.
“The fire service has arrived. Seeing the fire suddenly was truly terrifying,” he said.

item.title: Tarique, Takaichi begin bilateral summit in Tokyo
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi began their bilateral summit in Tokyo on Tuesday to strengthen the two countries’ strategic partnership, boost trade and investment, and expand cooperation in key sectors.
The talks began at 11:45am local time at the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office, known as the Kantei.
Earlier, Takaichi warmly welcomed Tarique at the Kantei upon his arrival. A contingent of the Japanese armed forces also accorded him a guard of honour.
After the ceremony, Takaichi introduced members of her cabinet to Tarique, who in turn introduced the members of his delegation to the Japanese Prime Minister.
The two leaders are scheduled to hold talks until 12:10pm. They will make a joint announcement on the outcome of their talks at 12:15pm.
Takaichi will later host a luncheon in honour of Tarique from 12:30pm to 1:10pm.
At the beginning of the lunch, she is scheduled to deliver a brief welcome remark and propose a toast, followed by a short reply and return toast from Tarique.
According to Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin, the two leaders will discuss strengthening bilateral relations, expanding business, trade and investment, Japanese cooperation in various sectors and international issues.
The two sides are also expected to explore cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.
Tarique is leading a high-level delegation comprising Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit and Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications, ICT and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad.
Other delegation members include Invest Bangladesh Authority Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Overseas Employment in Asia-Pacific Region Dr Md Shakirul Islam Khan, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam, Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury, Economic Relations Division Secretary Shahriar Kader Siddiky and Prime Minister’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon.
Hefazat-e-Islam Joint Secretary General and Nezame Islam Party acting Secretary General Azizul Haque Islamabadi and Am Janatar Dal General Secretary Md Tarek Rahman are also accompanying the Prime Minister.
The two countries’ national flags were displayed along the road leading to the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office to welcome Tarique.
Tarique then signed the visitors’ book at the entrance to the main hall of the building before the two leaders sat down for bilateral talks.
The Prime Minister arrived in Tokyo on Monday morning on a four-day visit at the invitation of Takaichi.
He was received at Narita International Airport by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Nakasone Yasutaka.
This is Tarique’s third state visit abroad since taking office on February 17 this year. He previously visited Malaysia and China on state visits and travelled to New York, the United States, in September to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

item.title: Sagar-Runi murder: Task force seeks more time to submit report
item.description:
A high-level task force formed under the Ministry of Home Affairs is verifying information gathered from various sources in connection with the murder of journalist couple Sagar Sarwar and Meherun Runi. The task force has sought more time from the High Court to submit its investigation report.
A progress report outlining the status of the investigation has already been submitted to the court.
The investigation report was scheduled to be submitted on Tuesday. The matter is before a High Court bench comprising Justice Shikdar Mahmudur Razi and Justice Fatema Anwar.
Ahead of the deadline, the task force filed an application for an extension, saying in its progress report that it was still verifying several pieces of information.
On September 30, 2024, the High Court ordered the removal of the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) from the investigation and directed the formation of a high-level task force under the Ministry of Home Affairs. The court initially set April 6, 2025, as the deadline for submitting the investigation report. The ministry subsequently formed the task force in line with the directive.
The report could not be submitted on the scheduled date, and the court later granted three six-month extensions following applications by the state, on April 22, October 23 and April 26. The case has now appeared on the High Court’s cause list again.
Sagar Sarwar, news editor at Maasranga Television, and Meherun Runi, a senior reporter at ATN Bangla, were murdered at their rented apartment in Dhaka’s West Rajabazar on the night of February 11, 2012. Their bodies were discovered the following morning.
The following day, Runi’s brother, Nausher Ali Roman, filed a murder case with Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station.
More than 14 years after the murders, the investigation report remains pending despite changes in the investigators and the formation of a high-level task force.

item.title: IFAD, partners support agritech startups to help small-scale farmers
item.description:
The International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the German Sparkassenstiftung for International Cooperation (DSIK) recently brought together startups, public institutions, market actors and development partners in Dhaka for the Innovatech Bangladesh Demo Day, marking the end of the programme's first cycle in Asia.
Funded by IFAD and the European Union and implemented by Sparkassenstiftung, Innovatech helps startups adapt, test and strengthen digital solutions for small-scale farmers.
In Bangladesh, two agritech startups, Agronochain and Krishi Shwapno, tested their solutions in the field alongside projects funded by IFAD and the government. The startups worked with the Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) and the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE).
At the Demo Day, the startups presented their implementation experiences, results and lessons. An accompanying panel discussion examined how institutions, market actors and financing mechanisms could work together to help solutions succeed in rural Bangladesh, move beyond pilot projects and reach more farmers.
“Transforming rural Bangladesh at the scale needed demands strong partnerships between government, innovators and the private sector,” said Valantine Achancho, IFAD country director for Bangladesh.
“Programmes like Innovatech complement public investment by bringing practical, market-driven solutions to rural communities. By testing new ideas and reducing investment risks, they help promising innovations grow into solutions that deliver lasting benefits for smallholder farmers and rural entrepreneurs,” he added.
“Rural areas do not need technology for technology’s sake. They need solutions that address a specific problem, work under the real conditions faced by producers and remain relevant after the project ends,” said Christina Olsen, director of Innovatech.
“At Innovatech, we start with demand and then bring startups and producers together so that solutions are adapted to the people who will actually use them,” she added.
The panel discussions highlighted that technology alone is rarely the main obstacle to expanding digital solutions in rural areas.
Moving from pilot projects to wider adoption requires genuine demand from rural communities, institutions willing to adopt the solutions, viable business models, market access and clear arrangements for financing and ownership after project support ends. The discussions also emphasised the need to engage the private sector as a full partner.
Bangladesh is part of Innovatech 2.0, which, between 2024 and 2026, helped more than 32,000 rural households in Bangladesh, Bolivia, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Peru access digital solutions developed by 15 technology startups.
The solutions help rural households connect with markets and financial services, manage crops, improve traceability and adopt more sustainable practices.
The programme connected the startups with 811 rural organisations, with nearly 17,000 women and more than 11,300 young people participating. Two out of every three participating producer organisations adopted agroecological practices.
Across its two editions, Innovatech has supported around 30 startups whose solutions have benefited more than 50,000 rural households.

Kane beats Yamal and Mbappe to taste Ballon d'Or glory
item.description:
Harry Kane became England's first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years in his native city of London on Monday, beating Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.
Alexia Putellas claimed the women's prize for a third time to extend Spain's domination of the award, thanks to her role in leading Barcelona to last season's Champions League before moving to London City Lionesses.
The first ever Ballon d'Or ceremony on English soil got off to an inauspicious start as the London traffic caused a delay of nearly an hour, with many of the star names arriving late.
But there was a happy ending for the hometown hero as Kane collected the crowning glory of his career to date, becoming the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.
The 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.
He also scored six times as England finished third at the World Cup.
"I love to represent my country and to bring this trophy back to them and have an English winner I think is something that's really, really special, especially here in London," Kane told AFP. "What a crazy night and I'm really, really happy."
Despite being England and Tottenham's all-time record goalscorer, Kane's medal collection is limited to German domestic triumphs.
He was on the losing side for Spurs in the 2019 Champions League final against Liverpool and twice tasted bitter defeat in the final of the European Championship with England.
But joining Bayern in 2023 and his remarkable goalscoring consistency have earned him the highest individual award in football.
"Making the move to Bayern Munich was a big step in my career," Kane told AFP earlier. "Some people saw it as a risk but for me it was always about improving and seeing if I could get better around the team-mates, the team, the club and it has pushed me onto another level.
"Being a number nine for Bayern and England you are expected to score goals and to do that the number of times I did last year is something I'm really proud of," he added.
The winner in 2021 and 2022, Putellas's third Ballon d'Or caps her return to the top of the women's game after an anterior cruciate ligament injury derailed her rise four years ago.
Putellas succeeds Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati, the winner the past three years whose season was quashed by a leg break.
"This is a consequence of all that we achieved last season," said Putellas.
"I am really grateful for having been (at Barcelona) 14 seasons as a player, it is something incredible. It was like a perfect story."
Yamal made the boldest fashion statement of the contenders with a pink flower on the front of his black suit.
The Barcelona winger scooped up the first award of the night for young talent of the year for the third consecutive time.
But the 19-year-old fell short of becoming the youngest ever Ballon d'Or winner, finishing third, after he failed to produce his best form during Spain's World Cup success.
Mbappe finished second but his wait to win the Ballon d'Or goes on despite being the top scorer in the World Cup, Champions League and La Liga as his goals did not lead to collective triumphs for France or Real Madrid.
Luis de la Fuente beat out Paris Saint-Germain's Luis Enrique and Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta to be named men's coach of the year after leading Spain to World Cup glory.
"This is recognition for a job very well done over many years," De la Fuente told AFP. "I believe Spanish football, both in terms of coaching and the game itself, serves as an example of excellent youth development, which ultimately paves the way for future success."
Barcelona's Pere Romeu scooped the prize for women's coach of the year.
Paris Saint-Germain missed out on any of the main individual awards despite winning a second consecutive Champions League, but did have the consolation of men's club of the year.
Spanish duo Unai Simon and Cata Coll were named best men's and women's goalkeeper.

item.title: Sakhawat: Govt plans major expansion of cancer care, radiotherapy facilities
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Monday said the government has taken steps to expand cancer treatment facilities across the country, with procurement of new radiotherapy and robotic surgery equipment underway.
“We are working fast to establish eight cancer institutes in the eight divisions and expand radiotherapy services at district level to ensure cancer treatment at the grassroots,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at the inaugural ceremony of the Medical Physics Program at Brac University in the city’s Merul Badda, Dhaka.
The Mathematics and Physical Sciences Department of Brac University introduced the two-year master's program for the first time in Bangladesh to meet the country’s growing demand for medical physicists.
About the government's commitment to ensure treatment for cancer, Sakhawat said the government has planned to procure 17 linear accelerators to make cancer treatment available across the country.
“We are also going to bring five major robotic surgery machines for the first time,” he said, emphasizing early detection and public awareness as critical components of the government’s cancer-control strategy, particularly for breast and cervical cancers.
He said the government would intensify HPV vaccination campaigns and promote breast cancer self-screening and awareness among women.
“Without awareness, we cannot save people from cancer,” Sakhawat said, urging health professionals and educational institutions to help spread awareness at the grassroots level.
Coming down heavily on the previous ‘fascist regime’, he said the ‘previous fascist government’ had destroyed the country’s health sector, which had been marred by corruption and plundering.
However, after assuming office, the present government has taken robust steps for the development of the country’s health sector, he said, adding that once the projects are implemented, the country would witness a revolutionary change in the health sector within the next two years.
“Under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, we are taking the healthcare services to village level,” the minister said, adding that the government planned to establish Family Wellbeing Centers in every three wards of each union and transform existing community clinics into Health Wellbeing Centers.
“These centers will provide primary-level services, including blood analysis and breast cancer screening,” he said.
Noting that every upazila hospital is going to be transformed into a 150-bed facility, the minister said the government will strengthen dialysis, physiotherapy, and maternal and newborn care at upazila-level hospitals to reduce pressure on tertiary healthcare facilities.
Stating that the government is going to appoint 5,000 doctors soon, Sakhawat said the government is also working to increase the number of hospital beds and recruit around 41,390 health workers, including 25,000 midwives, to strengthen healthcare delivery.
About the newly introduced program at Brac University, he assured government cooperation in developing medical physics education and manpower, saying the government would recruit medical physicists according to the needs of the expanding cancer treatment facilities.
“Medical physics is a very important part of treatment. You do your best and improve yourselves. From the government side, we must extend our hand of cooperation to you,” the minister said.
He said medical physicists play a crucial role in radiotherapy, as the accuracy of radiation dosage is vital for ensuring patient safety and the effectiveness of treatment.
“If the dose is wrong, the patient is gone. If the dose is wrong, the doctor’s credibility is gone,” he said, stressing the need to create adequate numbers of trained medical physicists.
He urged Brac University students, teachers and researchers to contribute to strengthening medical physics and cancer care in Bangladesh.
Professor Emeritus at Dhaka University Dr AFM Yusuf Haider, Additional Director General of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) Professor Dr Jalal Uddin Mohammad Rumi, Bangladesh Medical University (BMU) Clinical Oncology Department Chairman Professor Dr Syed Md Akram Hussain, National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital (NICRH) Director Professor Dr Mostafa Aziz Sumon and Project Director of Establishment of the Integrated Cancer, Kidney and Heart Treatment Centers across Bangladesh's Eight Divisional Cities Dr Md Toufiq Hasan Firoz spoke as special guests at the event.
Brac University Vice-Chancellor Professor Syed Ferhat Anwar chaired the program, while Mathematics and Physical Sciences (MPS) Department Chairperson Professor Hasibun Naher and Registrar and Controller of Examinations of the university Dr David Dowland delivered the welcome address.
Former Director and Chief Medical Physicist at Gummersbach University Hospital, University of Cologne in Germany, and Adviser and Coordinator of MPS at BRAC University, Professor Dr Golam Abu Zakaria presented the keynote paper, while Medical Physics Program Coordinator Professor Hasin Anupama Azhari presented an overview of the newly introduced program.

item.title: Bangladesh to showcase jute products at COP31 in Turkiye
item.description:
The government plans to showcase Bangladesh’s traditional jute and jute-made products at the UN climate conference COP31 in Turkiye to promote them in international markets.
A special exhibition of Bangladeshi jute products is planned at the Bangladesh pavilion during the conference, scheduled to take place in Antalya from November 9 to 20.
The initiative aims to promote jute as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic and highlight the commercial potential of Bangladesh’s jute industry.
Preparations are underway to display a range of jute products and related technologies at the pavilion. An exhibition display has been set up at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as part of the preparations.
The exhibition will showcase products such as jute bags, home décor items and handicrafts to international buyers, investors and policymakers.
Stakeholders believe growing global awareness of environmental pollution and the need for alternatives to plastic presents an opportunity to expand international markets for jute products.
As a natural, renewable and biodegradable fibre, jute has significant potential in environmentally friendly production and consumption.
At a meeting at the Foreign Ministry on October 15, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam highlighted the potential of Bangladesh’s jute industry during discussions on preparations for COP31 with climate experts and relevant stakeholders. The meeting emphasised promoting jute as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic.
If implemented, the initiative could help showcase the diverse uses of jute, explore new markets and strengthen commercial ties with foreign buyers, while bringing Bangladesh’s traditional “golden fibre” industry into the international spotlight.

item.title: Who will regulate the race for deep-sea resources?
item.description:
The growing race to exploit deep-sea resources is raising concerns over environmental damage, fragmented international oversight and accountability, as countries and companies seek minerals essential for batteries and clean energy technologies.
Polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts and polymetallic sulphides found on the ocean floor contain nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. While these resources could diversify mineral supplies, large-scale extraction could destroy seabed habitats, disturb sediments and threaten poorly understood marine ecosystems.
The central question is who will prevent environmental damage in international waters and hold those responsible accountable when harm occurs.
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) provides the principal legal framework for ocean governance. However, responsibility is divided among institutions overseeing seabed minerals, shipping, fisheries and marine biodiversity, creating challenges in coordinating environmental protection and enforcement.
The International Seabed Authority (ISA) regulates mineral-related activities in the international seabed Area beyond national jurisdiction. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) develops international standards for shipping safety and pollution prevention, while the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) supports sustainable fisheries management.
Although these institutions have distinct mandates, their activities can affect the same marine ecosystems. The combined effects of mining, shipping and fishing may remain difficult to assess when environmental data and monitoring systems are fragmented.
An activity could comply with one regulatory framework while contributing to environmental pressures that another institution does not adequately address. Establishing responsibility for damage becomes particularly difficult when several operators and regulatory systems are involved.
The Agreement on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, known as the BBNJ Agreement or High Seas Treaty, entered into force on January 17, 2026.
The agreement establishes a framework for marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, marine genetic resources and benefit-sharing, alongside capacity-building and technology transfer.
However, it does not replace the separate legal arrangements governing international seabed mining, shipping or fisheries. Coordination among existing institutions remains essential.
Effective implementation will require credible environmental assessments, transparent information-sharing, scientific monitoring and action against violations. The treaty's entry into force does not automatically guarantee effective conservation.
The challenge is particularly significant for developing countries, which often lack the research vessels, seabed sensors, specialised equipment and analytical capacity needed to independently monitor activities in distant international waters.
Without reliable baseline data and continuous monitoring, determining whether environmental changes result from a particular activity, natural processes, or other human pressures can be difficult.
Unequal access to scientific research and technology can also limit developing countries' ability to challenge environmental claims and participate meaningfully in international negotiations.
For Bangladesh, the issue is closely connected to the health of the Bay of Bengal, fisheries, coastal livelihoods and the country's blue economy.
The Bangladesh Oceanographic Research Institute (BORI) is conducting research on coastal marine resources, potential fishing habitats and marine pollution.
Abu Sharif Md Mahabub E Kibria, a marine scientist at BORI working on environmental and climate issues, said the institute was researching potentially valuable mineral resources along the coast, identifying potential fish habitats and detecting marine pollution in coastal and adjacent areas.
BORI is also working on extracting agar and carrageenan from seaweed and identifying suitable areas for seaweed cultivation in the sea.
These activities could strengthen Bangladesh's understanding of marine resources and environmental changes. However, coastal mineral exploration and mining in the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction involve different geographical areas, legal frameworks and environmental conditions.
Bangladesh's exclusive economic zone is legally distinct from international waters, where the country does not automatically exercise direct regulatory control. Nevertheless, marine pollution and ecological changes can cross maritime boundaries, affecting fisheries, food security and coastal economies.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Department of Fisheries and BORI could play important roles in monitoring international developments, strengthening scientific research and representing Bangladesh's interests in global negotiations.
Expanding access to marine data, developing research partnerships and improving technical expertise would help Bangladesh assess emerging risks and advocate for stronger environmental safeguards and fairer access to marine genetic resources.
Ultimately, the race for deep-sea resources cannot be governed by a single treaty or institution. Effective oversight will depend on coordination among regulatory bodies, transparent environmental assessments, reliable scientific evidence and clear procedures for investigating violations.
The challenge is not simply determining who can extract resources from the deep sea, but ensuring that economic benefits are shared fairly, environmental damage is prevented wherever possible and those responsible are held accountable.
Earlier, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said: "International cooperation and effective implementation of the BBNJ Agreement are important for protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction."
Then again, Leticia Carvalho, the ISA secretary-general, said: "Environmental protection, scientific evidence and effective regulatory oversight are central to governing international seabed mineral activities."
Even, Qu Dongyu, director-general of FAO, said: "Sustainable fisheries management requires science-based decisions, responsible harvesting and action against illegal fishing."
Expressing his opinion to Dhaka Tribune, Professor Ainun Nishat, an environmental and water resources expert, said: "Decisions on deep-sea resource extraction should account for environmental impacts, scientific evidence and long-term risks rather than economic potential alone."
Energy and environmental specialist Professor Ijaz Hossain from Buet, said: "Demand for minerals used in clean energy technologies should be considered alongside alternatives, recycling and safeguards against additional environmental damage."
Talking to Dhaka Tribune, Abu Sharif Md Mahabub E Kibria, marine scientist at BORI, said: "BORI is researching potential coastal mineral resources, fish habitats, marine pollution, seaweed-derived agar and carrageenan, and suitable areas for seaweed cultivation."
University of Dhaka oceanography and fisheries researchers and BORI marine scientists agreed that long-term research and regular monitoring are needed to assess deep-sea biodiversity and ecosystem risks, where scientific information remains limited; besides, scientific data and regional cooperation are important for understanding how changes in international waters could affect marine species, food webs and fisheries.

item.title: 21 BGB platoons deployed for Thakurgaon-1 by-election
item.description:
Twenty-one platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in the Thakurgaon-1 constituency ahead of the by-election to help ensure a free, fair and peaceful vote.
BGB personnel have been on duty in the constituency since Sunday, according to Thakurgaon Battalion (50 BGB).
The troops have been deployed across three upazilas, 22 unions and one municipality within the constituency. They will operate as mobile units and striking forces in their assigned areas.
Intelligence operations have also been intensified to strengthen security. At a press briefing, BGB officials said personnel were using body-worn cameras and drones to monitor key locations.
The force said its primary objective was to ensure that voters could cast their ballots safely and without obstruction.
Officials said BGB personnel are also monitoring the situation to ensure candidates have equal opportunities to campaign and that the electoral code of conduct is followed.
The force remains on alert to prevent unrest, violence and other activities that could threaten public safety during the election. Surveillance and patrols have also been strengthened in border areas.

item.title: Writ filed seeking halt to illegal sand extraction from Padma
item.description:
A writ petition has been filed with the High Court seeking to stop illegal and unplanned sand extraction from the Padma River, citing concerns over riverbank erosion, environmental damage and the safety of the Padma Bridge and its associated infrastructure.
Dr Md Golam Rahman Bhuiyan, chairman of human rights and social development organisation Manobadhikar O Samaj Unnayan Sangstha (MOSUS), filed the public interest petition on Monday. He is also a lawyer and human rights activist.
The petition raises concerns that illegal, unplanned sand extraction could alter the river's natural course, weaken its banks, and damage the surrounding environment and biodiversity. It also warns of potential risks to important national infrastructure, including the Padma Bridge.
It seeks High Court directives requiring the relevant government authorities to fulfil their legal responsibilities, investigate allegations of illegal sand extraction, take legal action against those responsible and implement effective measures to prevent further violations.
The Padma River plays a vital role in Bangladesh's economy, environment, agriculture and fisheries, as well as in the livelihoods of communities along its banks. Disruptions to its natural flow and ecological balance could threaten agricultural land, natural resources and the people who depend on the river.
The petition also highlights the need for scientific assessments and regular monitoring to evaluate the potential impact of sand extraction on the river and the safety of the Padma Bridge and related infrastructure.
MOSUS said the relevant authorities must take effective steps to protect natural resources, uphold environmental justice and ensure the rule of law.
Through the public interest litigation, the organisation seeks judicial intervention to ensure that the authorities take lawful and effective measures to protect the Padma River.

item.title: PM arrives in Tokyo on four-day state visit to Japan
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrived in Tokyo on Monday morning on a four-day state visit to Japan at the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
A Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and other members of the entourage landed at Narita International Airport at 9:05am local time, according to the Prime Minister's Office.
At the airport, the prime minister was received by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Yasutaka Nakasone.
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Rehan Asif Asad, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Overseas Employment in the Asia-Pacific Region Shakirul Islam Khan and senior officials of the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo were also present.
He was later taken to the Imperial Hotel, where he will stay during the visit, in a ceremonial motorcade.
Earlier, the flight departed from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 12:10am Bangladesh time.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Prime Minister’s Political Adviser and BNP acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, Chief Whip Nurul Islam Moni and Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani saw the Prime Minister and his wife off at the VIP lounge of the Dhaka airport.
The prime minister is leading a small delegation during the visit.
The delegation includes Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Finance and Planning Adviser Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, Invest Bangladesh Authority Executive Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam, Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury and Economic Relations Division Secretary Md Shahriar Kader Siddiky.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are scheduled to hold a high-level formal meeting on Tuesday morning.
A joint declaration will be issued after the meeting.
Later, the prime minister and members of his delegation will attend a luncheon hosted by the Japanese prime minister.
During the visit, Tarique Rahman will hold talks with Japanese government officials, development institutions and business leaders, visit industrial and energy facilities, and deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum.
The visit is expected to deepen the existing strategic partnership, attract fresh Japanese investment, expand trade and accelerate ongoing development projects, said Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam while speaking at a curtain-raiser media briefing at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 20.
Discussions will focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.
The two sides will also explore wider cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.
The prime minister’s tentative programmes include engagements with the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League and the chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation.
Meetings are also being planned with the president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and the chairman of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation.
The foreign secretary said the two sides are discussing draft memoranda of understanding (MoU) and cooperation agreements covering agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, trade, environmental conservation and local government modernisation.
"We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit," he said.
Around eight MoUs are under discussion, of which three to four could be signed during the visit. Separate agreements are also being pursued in education and human resource development.
Detailed discussions are planned on Japanese support for establishing factories in Bangladesh, generating employment and developing human resources in line with the prime minister's priorities.
The two sides are also expected to discuss regional and international peace and stability, a sustainable and peaceful solution to the Rohingya crisis, stronger cooperation in addressing the energy crisis and efforts to end international conflicts.
The visit follows the prime minister's participation in an online meeting in April at the invitation of the Japanese prime minister, during which Bangladesh welcomed a Japan-led initiative to address energy challenges across Asia.
